siteMetadata.about:
I’m Nezar, a Data Scientist in Paris working on LLM and NLP systems in production. I hold an engineering degree in Applied Mathematics and Computer Science from Polytech Sorbonne.
        I scope, build and own production LLM pipelines on Databricks and PySpark, evaluating models against hand-annotated benchmarks rather than spot-checks. Beyond that my work spans retrieval-augmented QA, fraud detection under extreme class imbalance, recommender systems, and time-series forecasting.
        In my free time, I enjoy long-distance running, traveling, and discovering new places, always on the lookout for fresh challenges to learn and grow.

markdownRemark.html:
In this post, we’ll see why Cochran’s formula can only be derived for statistics based on the sample mean, and then show how the same logic gives the formula for proportions.

1. The Central Limit Theorem: Foundation of Statistical Inference

The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) states that if

X1,X2,…,XmX_1, X_2, \dots, X_mX1​,X2​,…,Xm​

are independent, identically distributed random variables with

E[Xi]=μ,Var(Xi)=σ2<∞,E[X_i] = \mu,\quad \mathrm{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty,E[Xi​]=μ,Var(Xi​)=σ2<∞,

then as (m \to \infty),

m (Xˉm−μ)  →d  N(0, σ2).\sqrt{m}\,\bigl(\bar X_m - \mu\bigr) \;\xrightarrow{d}\; N(0,\,\sigma^2).m​(Xˉm​−μ)d​N(0,σ2).

Key conditions:

  • Finite mean (μ\muμ)
  • Bounded variance (σ2\sigma^2σ2)

2. Properties of the Normal Distribution and Critical Values

Let Z∼N(0,1)Z \sim N(0,1)Z∼N(0,1). For a confidence level 1−α1 - \alpha1−α, define the critical value zα/2z_{\alpha/2}zα/2​ by

P(Z>zα/2)=α2.P\bigl(Z > z_{\alpha/2}\bigr) = \frac{\alpha}{2}.P(Z>zα/2​)=2α​.
  • For 95% confidence (α=0.05\alpha = 0.05α=0.05), z0.025=1.96z_{0.025} = 1.96z0.025​=1.96.

  • Then

    P(−zα/2<Z<zα/2)=1−α.P\bigl(-z_{\alpha/2} < Z < z_{\alpha/2}\bigr) = 1 - \alpha.P(−zα/2​<Z<zα/2​)=1−α.

3. From Sample Mean to Confidence Intervals

By the CLT,

Xˉ−μσ/m∼N(0,1),\frac{\bar X - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{m}} \sim N(0,1),σ/m​Xˉ−μ​∼N(0,1),

so

P ⁣(−zα/2<Xˉ−μσ/m<zα/2)=1−α.P\!\Bigl(-z_{\alpha/2} < \tfrac{\bar X - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{m}} < z_{\alpha/2}\Bigr) = 1 - \alpha.P(−zα/2​<σ/m​Xˉ−μ​<zα/2​)=1−α.

Rearrange to isolate (μ\muμ) :

P ⁣(Xˉ−zα/2 σm<μ<Xˉ+zα/2 σm)=1−α.P\!\Bigl(\bar X - z_{\alpha/2}\,\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{m}} < \mu < \bar X + z_{\alpha/2}\,\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{m}}\Bigr) = 1 - \alpha.P(Xˉ−zα/2​m​σ​<μ<Xˉ+zα/2​m​σ​)=1−α.

The margin of error is

E=zα/2 σm.E = z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{m}}.E=zα/2​m​σ​.

4. Cochran’s Key Insight: Flipping the Perspective

Instead of computing the interval after sampling, Cochran asked:

“How many samples do I need for a given (E)?”

Rearrange

E=zα/2 σmE = z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{m}}E=zα/2​m​σ​

to solve for m :

m=(zα/2)2 σ2E2.m = \frac{(z_{\alpha/2})^2\,\sigma^2}{E^2}.m=E2(zα/2​)2σ2​.

⚠️ Note: This derivation depends critically on the CLT for the sample mean, so only applies when your statistic is a mean (i.e. when you know or estimate (σ2\sigma^2σ2) .

5. Cochran’s Formula for Estimating Proportions

The same logic applied to a Bernoulli variable (Xi \in {0,1}) with (P(Xi = 1) = p) yields the formula for proportions:

  • Sample proportion:

    p^=1m∑i=1mXi.\hat p = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m X_i.p^​=m1​i=1∑m​Xi​.

  • Moments:

    E[p^]=p,Var(p^)=p(1−p)m.E[\hat p] = p,\quad \mathrm{Var}(\hat p) = \frac{p(1-p)}{m}.E[p^​]=p,Var(p^​)=mp(1−p)​.

  • CLT →

    p^−pp(1−p)/m∼N(0,1),\frac{\hat p - p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/m}} \sim N(0,1),p(1−p)/m​p^​−p​∼N(0,1),

    so

    E=zα/2 p(1−p)m⟹m=p(1−p) (zα/2)2E2.E = z_{\alpha/2}\,\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{m}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad m = \frac{p(1-p)\,(z_{\alpha/2})^2}{E^2}.E=zα/2​mp(1−p)​​⟹m=E2p(1−p)(zα/2​)2​.
  • If (p) is unknown, set (p = 0.5) to maximize (p(1-p)) and obtain the most conservative (largest) sample size.

With these derivations in hand, you can choose your margin of error (E) and confidence level (1-\alpha) to compute exactly how many observations you need—whether you’re estimating a mean or a proportion.

frontmatter.description: Step-by-step derivation of Cochran’s formula, showing why it applies only to sample means and how it extends to proportions.
